headline: A wave of cyberattacks on South Korean banks and Japanese companies shows how AI may be making hacking easier for people with little technical skill, experts told Reuters.
score_reason: Pool score kept: it widens the story to Japan with figures and official responses, but AI's role is still under investigation in many cases and the main facts overlap with C12-01.
importance_line: Customers and staff of South Korean banks and Japanese firms such as Daiwa Securities, SoftBank and Lawson face higher risk of phishing and data misuse, and regulators in both countries are responding, but authorities have not yet confirmed whether or how AI was used in many of the breaches.
summary: Reuters reports that cyberattacks possibly aided by AI tools are under investigation at nine South Korean banks and two mega-churches, and that a surge of incidents has hit Japanese firms including Daiwa Securities, SoftBank Corp and the Lawson convenience-store chain, though in many cases officials have not yet established whether or how AI played a part. This continues our 6 Oct 2026 report that South Korea's president said signs of AI use had emerged in the bank hacks; new today are CrowdStrike's view that the suspected China-based attacker probably could not have run the campaign without AI, South Korea's order for a 12-point security self-assessment across finance, and a meeting of Japanese ministries on Thursday.
notes: Reuters page (HTTP 401) not openable; Reuters text read on the KELO-AM copy; link kept at the Reuters original. Same story line as C12-01 (CrowdStrike findings); the dedupe step may treat the Korea facts as overlapping.
